summary: This was the week two storylines that had been building since early September came to a head at once. A synchronized global hiking cycle -- the Fed's first hike since 2023 on Wednesday, the BOJ's hike to a three-decade high on Friday, and a hawkish BoE hold sandwiched between them, all layered on the ECB's early-September move -- drove sovereign yields to multi-decade highs in the US, UK, Germany and Japan simultaneously. At the same time, the Gulf's twin chokepoint crisis hardened from an open question into a settled, asymmetric fact: Saudi Arabia effectively cut Europe out of crude and diesel supply through October while quietly protecting its Asian long-term contracts in full, turning a shared geopolitical risk into a one-sided European inflation shock. The AI trade whiplashed within the week itself -- Monday opened in crisis (Amodei's AI-safety warning, SoftBank's 11% plunge, a Samsung/SK Hynix selloff) and the week closed in euphoria, with Nvidia and Broadcom's bullish demand commentary driving the Kospi to a fresh record above 6,890 by Friday on the same underlying AI-capex story. Central banks also moved in lockstep but the market read each hike differently: the Fed's was treated as hawkish and durable, while the BOJ's was read as dovish because of its unusual 7-2 dissent, which weakened rather than strengthened the yen. Underneath it all, Beijing spent the week manufacturing calm -- an eight-session yuan-strengthening streak and a 16th straight rate hold -- ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, even as fresh signs of property-sector distress (a scrapped Beijing land auction, a regulatory setback on developer debt) kept accumulating. A reader who followed each day in isolation would have whiplashed between panic and relief on both AI and oil; the throughline is that neither story actually resolved this week -- they just rotated which asset class was absorbing the stress.

themes.title: Gulf chokepoint crisis hardens into a one-sided European supply shock
themes.detail: The week opened with the Oman-hosted Iran-GCC talks postponed indefinitely and Houthi forces capturing the Hanish Islands to tighten their grip on Bab el-Mandeb, while Saudi Arabia's drone-damaged East-West pipeline stayed shut. By midweek Saudi Arabia signaled the pipeline could partially restart within days, easing oil prices -- but by Thursday and Friday the story inverted: Aramco cancelled all remaining September and October crude allocations to at least three European refiners after fresh strikes hit the Yanbu export hub, sending gasoil crack spreads to a record $79/bbl and the Forties-to-Brent premium from $0.50 to $15 in weeks. Reporting into the weekend confirmed Asian buyers are still receiving full contracted volumes, meaning Aramco chose to absorb the entire disruption on Europe's side -- a genuine geographic bifurcation of the same crisis rather than a shared global shock.

themes.title: Fed, BOJ and BoE all move in the same week, but markets read the hikes in opposite directions
themes.detail: The Fed delivered its first hike since 2023 (to 3.75-4.00%) on Wednesday with a hawkish dot plot showing 16 of 18 officials expecting more tightening, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5% and the dollar to its best week since June. The BOJ hiked to 1.25% -- its highest since 1995 -- on Friday, but a 7-2 dissent vote was read as diluting the pace of future tightening, so the yen weakened through 157 instead of rallying, even as the Nikkei jumped on the exporter-friendly currency move. The Bank of England held at 3.75% on a hawkish 6-3 split, whipsawing gilts from near-1998 highs to a sharp relief rally and back. Bund yields hit their highest since 2009 and gilts their highest since 2007 by week's end, confirming a genuinely globally synchronized -- if inconsistently interpreted -- tightening cycle.

themes.title: The AI trade crashes and rallies on the same underlying story within a single week
themes.detail: Monday's session opened with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's 'We Must Pace the Frontier' warning, backed by Altman and Musk, triggering a genuine cross-asset tech selloff: SoftBank fell 11.4% on Altman's confirmation OpenAI would skip a 2026 IPO, and Samsung and SK Hynix dropped 4-6% as Kospi posted its worst session in a month. By Friday the same AI-capex complex had fully reversed, with Nvidia's Jensen Huang predicting twice as many AI chip sales in 2027 and Broadcom calling demand 'very strong and durable,' sending SK Hynix up 6.4%, Samsung up 3.4%, and the Kospi to a record 6,894 -- up more than 55% year-to-date. The whiplash illustrates how thin and headline-driven positioning has become across the memory and AI-hardware complex.

themes.title: Beijing engineers currency calm into the Trump-Xi summit while property stress keeps building underneath
themes.detail: The PBOC guided the yuan to its strongest level since mid-2022 through an eight-session streak of firmer fixings, and held loan prime rates unchanged for a 16th straight month, prioritizing currency and diplomatic optics ahead of the September 24 Trump-Xi summit over any domestic stimulus push. Chinese tech names (Alibaba, PDD, JD.com) rallied 3-4% into the weekend on summit positioning. Underneath that managed calm, the property sector's problems kept accumulating rather than resolving: regulators declined to register developers' convertible bonds, a Beijing land auction drew no real bids, and China Vanke's restructuring dragged on all week -- a reminder that the currency-stability push is papering over, not fixing, the credit overhang.
